strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: learning preferences from naturally occurring, multi-turn user feedback. The pipeline connects feedback detection, preference summarization, response generation, and preference training, producing a substantial dataset of 20,281 expert-response pairs.

Table 3 provides meaningful evidence of training utility across three model families and several established benchmarks. With GPT-4-generated data, AlpacaEval length-controlled win rates improve from 24.3% to 34.9% for Phi 3, 22.9% to 34.2% for LLaMA 3, and 17.1% to 31.4% for Mistral. These gains support a useful empirical contribution beyond the proposed evaluator.

The authors validate feedback detection using four human annotators on 50 conversations, report agreement and classification metrics, and explicitly separate evaluation users and conversations from training. The appendices provide detailed rubrics, annotation and evaluation prompts, model identifiers, and principal training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the contribution of in-situ feedback. Comparisons are primarily against models without additional training; there is no matched GPT-4 distillation baseline without feedback guidance, SFT-only ablation, or comparison with an existing preference dataset under comparable training budgets. Expert and on-policy variants also differ in dataset size, response provenance, and filtering. Consequently, the gains cannot be attributed specifically to authentic feedback rather than additional training or stronger teacher responses.

The central claim of improved alignment with actual users lacks independent validation. GPT-4 identifies feedback, summarizes preferences, generates expert responses, filters on-policy pairs, and judges the proposed evaluation. Figure 2 shows that supplying these summaries changes GPT-4's rankings, but does not establish greater agreement with users. Human validation covers SAT/DSAT detection only; it does not assess summary fidelity, generated pair correctness, or the modified evaluator. Correlation previously reported for WildBench does not establish validity for this adaptation.

The evidence for representative user preferences is limited. Only approximately 12.8% of conversations contain detected feedback, and DSAT recall is 48.4% despite 83.3% precision (Table 6). The evaluation additionally selects preferences most similar to others within task clusters and deliberately favors tasks resembling training data. This supports conclusions about selected, typical interactions, while leaving population coverage and minority preferences unresolved. The acknowledged selection bias substantially qualifies claims about diverse or 'true' human values.

The interpretation of results overstates their consistency. Section 5 claims that neither dataset variant compromises benchmark performance, yet on-policy Mistral declines on AlpacaEval LC (17.1% to 12.9%), Arena-Hard (12.6% to 10.3%), and MT-Bench (6.71 to 6.42). No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run results accompany claims of significant improvement, which particularly affects small changes such as GPT-4-trained Mistral's MT-Bench increase from 6.71 to 6.79.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful appendix details. The manuscript only promises a future dataset release and provides no implementation or split artifacts. Important construction details—including clustering embeddings, precise deduplication and filtering rules, and generation settings—are unspecified. It should also state explicitly whether preference system prompts are retained during training or supplied during evaluation generation. Together with the missing controlled comparisons and independent validation, these gaps warrant substantive revision before a Findings recommendation.
